subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Apollo 11: Walking on the Moon
description: One-minute skill: Apollo 11: Walking on the Moon.

hook.text: On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon. 600 million people watched live on television.

buildup.text: Kennedy had pledged to reach the Moon by the end of the decade. NASA achieved it with just five months to spare.

discovery.text: Armstrong and Aldrin spent 2.5 hours on the surface. They collected rocks, planted a flag, and left footprints that remain today.

twist.text: The landing almost failed. Armstrong had to manually fly past a boulder field with just 25 seconds of fuel remaining.

climax.text: Twelve people walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972. No one has returned since—but Artemis aims to change that.

punchline.text: Twelve walked on the Moon. Their footprints will last millions of years.

quiz.question: How close did Apollo 11 come to running out of fuel during the Moon landing?
options: Armstrong had only about 25 seconds of fuel left when he landed
They had plenty of fuel—the landing went exactly as planned
They ran out of fuel and had to abort the first attempt

details.summary: On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first humans to walk on the Moon while Michael Collins orbited above. Armstrong's 'one small step' was watched by 600 million people — the largest television audience in history at that time.
details.whyItMatters: Apollo 11 fulfilled a seemingly impossible goal within a decade and demonstrated what humanity can achieve through science, engineering, and determination.
takeaways: Armstrong and Aldrin walked on the Moon on July 20, 1969
600 million people worldwide watched the historic event live
Returned Moon rocks transformed lunar and planetary science

faq.question: What did we learn from the Moon rocks?
faq.answer: Apollo missions returned 382 kilograms of lunar samples. Analysis revealed the Moon formed from debris after a Mars-sized body struck early Earth (the giant impact hypothesis).

faq.question: Why haven't humans returned to the Moon since 1972?
faq.answer: Apollo was driven by Cold War competition, not sustained scientific interest. After winning the Space Race, political will and funding evaporated. The enormous cost, risk, and lack of clear economic return made return missions hard to justify.
